edits.category: Explanation of packet splitting and filtered cancellation
edits.before:
A direct packet decomposition and a filtration behave differently.  In a direct sum of subcomplexes, cohomology splits packet by packet.  In a filtration, a class visible at one graded depth can be killed by a later differential.


There are two different mechanisms for a coarse obstruction to vanish.  The first is packetwise vanishing.  Every fine class is already zero.  The second is cancellation through compatibility.  Fine classes are nonzero, but later differentials pair them and remove them before the total cohomology is reached.  A direct sum decomposition allows only the first mechanism.  A filtration can allow both.
edits.after:
A direct packet decomposition splits a complex into independent pieces, so cohomology splits packet by packet. A filtration retains relations between depths. Its associated graded cohomology can contain classes that disappear on later pages of a spectral sequence.

There are therefore two ways for fine obstruction data to give zero total obstruction. Each fine class may already vanish, or later differentials may remove nonzero classes through compatibility between depths. Only the first mechanism occurs in a direct sum of subcomplexes. A filtration can exhibit both.

\begin{interpretation}[title={Lifting and survival answer different questions}]
A depth obstruction tests whether a chosen approximation admits one further correction. A spectral sequence follows cohomology classes of a filtered complex through later differentials. Turning successive corrections into an exact solution also uses compatible choices, completeness, continuity, and separatedness.

edits.before: Local solvability appears here as the existence of every edge map.  Global solvability asks whether all local frames can be chosen at once. edits.category: Connected prose for the limits of the calculus
edits.before: Several limits remain explicit.  Exact packet coordinates are a representation theorem, not a general solution theorem.  The cokernel is canonical relative to the correction map, but the correction map itself belongs to the problem data.  The cokernel may be infinite dimensional.  A split Hilbert projector requires closed range.  Coarse vanishing can erase a nonzero fine obstruction.  A vanishing linear obstruction does not remove higher nonlinear terms.  A spectral sequence records possible cancellation, but it does not force cancellation.  Finite graph holonomy and smooth projector transport do not establish a continuum field theory.
edits.after:
Exact packet coordinates give a representation of the data. Solving the associated problem still requires the correction and lifting hypotheses. The correction map belongs to the problem data, and its cokernel is canonical relative to that choice. The cokernel may be infinite dimensional. In the Hilbert setting, the orthogonal obstruction projector requires closed range.

Coarse vanishing can erase a nonzero fine obstruction, and higher nonlinear terms can obstruct a problem whose linear class vanishes. A spectral sequence records which classes survive the later differentials. An application of finite graph holonomy or smooth projector transport to a continuum field theory requires the additional realization data just described.

edits.category: Final prose on what the obstruction objects record
edits.before: These results do not assert that all obstructions vanish.  Nonlinear continuation failures can be placed in exact quotient or cohomology objects whenever a correction problem is specified.  Those objects admit packet decomposition, filtered refinement, natural transport, and holonomy tests under explicit hypotheses.
edits.after: Whenever a nonlinear continuation problem supplies a correction map, its residual can be recorded in an exact quotient or cohomology object. Under the stated hypotheses, these objects admit packet decomposition, filtered refinement, natural transport, and holonomy tests. They identify the obstruction that a correction or gluing step must address.
